claims.locator: Why accurate diagnosis is critical; Diagnostic criteria for AOM
claims.statement: AOM requires acute symptoms, middle-ear effusion, and significant acute middle-ear inflammation; a bulging tympanic membrane is the most predictive inflammatory sign.
Otitis media with effusion has middle-ear effusion without signs of acute middle-ear inflammation and must be distinguished from AOM.
Ear pain may reflect viral myringitis or eustachian-tube dysfunction with decreased hearing rather than AOM.
Otitis externa causes external-canal pain with tragal movement and canal inflammation, usually without systemic symptoms, and must be distinguished from AOM-associated drainage.
Important stridor alternatives include bacterial tracheitis, deep neck infection, epiglottitis, foreign-body aspiration, and acute allergic reaction, each with source-listed distinguishing features.

Naltrexone and acamprosate are first-line pharmacotherapies for moderate or severe AUD; naltrexone supports abstinence or reduction, acamprosate supports abstinence, and current or expected opioid use contraindicates naltrexone.
Topiramate or gabapentin may be offered when first-line medications do not benefit the patient, are contraindicated, or the patient prefers an alternative; selection remains individualized.
